title: Board lenses — By status | By theme | By dependency
description:
One switcher at the top of the ideas page that re-groups the same cards without changing any data: by status (today's columns), by theme, or by dependency tier. The board stops being one opinionated layout and becomes several readings of the same backlog.

Technical shape: a lens chip row beside Active/Archive; grouping is a pure function from lens → array of {label, ideas}, with the existing column renderer drawing whatever it's handed. Status lens keeps the burner split; theme lens groups by config vocab (untagged last); dependency lens defers to the tiering idea. Lens choice remembered per browser like the board's Epics/Rows toggle.
context: The current columns mix two taxonomies — front/back burner is priority, ready-for-review/ready-to-implement is maturity — which the user flagged as manageable at ~20 ideas but incoherent as a single axis. Lenses resolve that without forcing a column restructure: keep the status columns as the default reading, and let priority or dependency become the grouping when that's the question being asked.
compounding: The grouping abstraction is what makes the dependency view cheap, and any future lens (by milestone, by conviction, by owner) becomes a function rather than a feature.
pros: Sidesteps the column-taxonomy problem instead of forcing a migration
Each new lens is a small pure function once the switcher exists
Keeps today's default view exactly as it is
cons: Three ways to look at one board can itself be a decision cost
The status columns' drag-to-change-status behaviour only makes sense in the status lens — other lenses must be read-only or define their own drop semantics

log.note: Captured from the user's design critique, which proposed the lens row and explicitly deferred the column-taxonomy change ('I would not force this change yet'). This is the non-destructive path to the same benefit.
Enriched for agent pickup: why-now, the open decision, conviction, build constraints and an acceptance boundary — so a builder can judge scope without reconstructing the reasoning from prose.

Shipped. The lens switcher and the grouping abstraction landed with the leverage view (idea-dependency-view), which needed them to exist. Grouping is a pure function from lens to groups with the existing card renderer drawing whatever it is handed, as the constraints required; the Status lens renders exactly as before, drag and burner split included. Theme shipped too — it was ten lines once the abstraction existed, which was the argument for the abstraction. Built directly rather than promoted to an epic first (user instruction).

why_now: The idea columns mix two taxonomies — front/back burner is priority, ready-for-review/ready-to-implement is maturity — judged manageable at ~20 ideas; arc is now past 60.
decision: In a non-status lens, is drag disabled entirely, or does each lens define its own drop semantics?
constraints: Grouping must be a pure function from lens to [{label, ideas}] with the existing column renderer drawing whatever it is handed; the status lens must render exactly as it does today.
acceptance: Switching lenses regroups the same cards with no data written, and the default view is indistinguishable from the current page.

title: Claim hygiene — sessions end, claims don't
description:
A claimed card whose agent walked away looks like work in flight forever. Surface stale claims where they live (a dim 'claimed 3d ago' on the card itself), give the human a one-click release, and let an agent clear its own claims when it stops.

Technical shape: the briefing already computes staleness (claimed_at > 48h, not done) — lift that into a shared staleClaims() and render an age hint on cards/story chips past the threshold, with a 'release claim' action in the modal that nulls claimed_by/claimed_at. Contract side: AGENTS.md §6 gains 'clear your claim when you stop working a card, even mid-story'. No new fields, no server change.
context: PROTOCOL §3 makes 'already claimed' a reason a card is unpickable — so a stale claim silently removes work from the queue, and the ready-queue's empty state says 'claimed, in flight, or behind a gate/dep' without saying which. This session created the problem at scale: every epic and story it touched still carries claimed_by 'claude (this session)', a session that no longer exists. Multiply by every future agent run.
compounding: Makes the selection rule trustworthy — the one property everything else (next-up, ready queue, briefing, any future dispatch) reads. Cheap now because the briefing already detects staleness; the same signal becomes the seed of any board-health surface.
pros: The detection logic already exists (briefing) — this is surfacing plus one write
Directly protects PROTOCOL §3's pickability from silent rot
Closes a gap this very session created on two boards
cons: 48h is a guess at a threshold; may want it configurable later (deliberately not now — simplest thing first)

log.note: Captured from the session retrospective: after two days of agent-driven card movement, every touched card carries a claim from a dead session. The board's own dogfooding surfaced it.
Enriched for agent pickup: why-now, the open decision, conviction, build constraints and an acceptance boundary — so a builder can judge scope without reconstructing the reasoning from prose.

User directed 'execute on the next card' in conversation — the thumbs-up. Ranked next by the decision lens: the only quick win on the board (low effort, high impact) and the one blocking the selection rule's trustworthiness. Promoted to B21.

why_now: Sessions now end with claims stranded across two boards; PROTOCOL §4.7 tells agents to release theirs, but nothing surfaces the ones already stuck — and a stale claim silently removes work from the ready queue.
decision: Is 48h the right staleness threshold, and should releasing a claim be one click or require confirmation?
constraints: No new fields — reuse claimed_at and the briefing's existing staleness computation. Advisory only: never auto-clear a claim, because a long-running job is indistinguishable from an abandoned one.
acceptance: A card claimed by a session that has ended shows how long it has been held, and can be released in one action from the board; the ready queue stops hiding pickable work behind dead claims.

title: Bulk actions — stop clicking thirteen times
description:
Select several cards (shift-click or a checkbox mode) and act once: archive, move lane, set priority/milestone/theme, release claims. The board is agent-fast to write and human-slow to curate; this closes that gap.

Technical shape: a selection Set in memory, a `.selected` outline, and a small action bar that appears when the set is non-empty; each action loops the existing single-card mutation (archive/move/field-set) then persists once. Escape or empty-space click clears. Rows mode selects stories, epics mode selects epics — no cross-type selection.
context: Curation is inherently plural — 'archive everything shipped', 'move these four to Next', 'clear the dead claims' — but every affordance is singular. This session archived thirteen completed epics by writing a Python loop against the JSON, because doing it in the UI meant thirteen modal round-trips; a human without an agent has no such escape hatch.
compounding: Bulk archive is what makes ship-and-archive (B13) survive contact with a year-old board; bulk claim-release pairs with claim hygiene. Selection itself is reusable — any future action gets multi-apply for free.
pros: Makes curation practical for humans, not just agents with a shell
Reuses every existing mutation — the loop is the feature
cons: Selection UI is new interaction surface on a board whose interaction model is deliberately small (drag + click)
Only pays off on boards big enough to have plural work — arc-scale, not new-project scale

log.note: Captured from the session retrospective: archiving 13 finished epics required a script, which is a fine agent path and a terrible human one.
Enriched for agent pickup: why-now, the open decision, conviction, build constraints and an acceptance boundary — so a builder can judge scope without reconstructing the reasoning from prose.

why_now: Archiving thirteen finished epics took a Python loop — an acceptable agent path and an impossible human one; the ship-and-archive lifecycle makes that plural work routine.
decision: Is selection a distinct mode you enter, or ambient shift-click on the existing cards?
constraints: Every bulk action loops an existing single-card mutation and persists once — no new write paths that could diverge from the single-card rules.
acceptance: Several cards can be archived, moved or re-prioritised in one gesture, and the result is identical to doing them one at a time.

title: Next-up panel — the selection rule in the UI
description: A ranked 'pickable now' strip on the board implementing PROTOCOL §3, which today exists only agent-side. Shows each pick's why: priority tier, then unblock count.
context: The board's core question — what should be worked on next — is answered by a rule the UI never shows. A human opening the board has to re-derive pickability (first lane, deps done, gate open, unclaimed, WIP under limit) by eye. The rule is already specified and all inputs are client-side; this is pure rendering.
compounding: Once pickability is computed in the page, the WIP/gate surfacing and ready-queue ideas reuse the same function — three UI ideas share one implementation of PROTOCOL §3.
pros: Rule and data already exist; no server change
Human and agent finally see the same answer to 'what's next'
Foundation for WIP/gate badges and the ready queue
cons: Selection rule now lives in two places (PROTOCOL.md prose and JS) — drift risk unless the spec framework covers it

log.note: Captured from the capability brainstorm: quick win — the tool's central rule is invisible to its human customer.

Built, ad hoc (no epic/milestone): #nextup strip on the board page implements PROTOCOL §3 exactly — pickability (first lane, deps done, gate open, unclaimed, WIP) ranked by priority → unblock count → file order, with a reasons line when nothing is pickable. First real exercise of the Design workflow: design/board.md updated with the code. First UI reader of open_gates and wip_limits.

title: Board briefing — 'since you last looked'
description:
A digest when you open the board: what changed since you last looked — new cards, lane moves, ideas that advanced, stale claims (claimed but motionless for days), newly blocked or unblocked cards. The session-break catch-up, computed instead of remembered.

Technical shape: reuses the ratify panel's git-read endpoint and semantic JSON differ, pointed at the last-seen commit instead of HEAD. The client remembers last-seen as a commit hash (localStorage, per browser, like the board-mode memory); the server diffs the two snapshots into the same card-level statements, grouped new / moved / advanced / stale; stale claims computed from claimed_at age. Dismissing the briefing just updates the stored hash — nothing written to the board.
context: Agents edit the board between the human's visits — and now move cards in real time while building, so the volume of between-visit change keeps growing. Today the human diffs mentally or reads git log by hand. A briefing turns the board from a static snapshot into a conversation that resumes where it left off — the same trust story as the ratify panel, applied to session boundaries instead of commits.
compounding: Second consumer of the git-read endpoint + differ (after the ratify panel) — the pair amortizes fast. Stale-claim and newly-blocked detection are reusable signals: the same checks feed any future board-health surface or agent watchdog.
pros: Serves the real usage pattern: agent works, human reviews later
Cheap once the git endpoint exists
cons: Needs a notion of 'last looked' (localStorage timestamp) — slightly stateful
Depends on ratify-review's git endpoint to be cheap

log.note: Captured from the capability brainstorm. Sequenced after idea-ratify-review — reuses its git endpoint.

Promoted Later → Next: once the ratify review panel ships its git-read endpoint + semantic differ, the briefing is the same machinery pointed at an older commit — its effective effort drops from medium to low.

Hardened: description restructured to plain + Technical shape (last-seen commit hash in localStorage, reuse of ratify differ, new/moved/advanced/stale grouping); context tied to real-time card movement; compounding extended to board-health signals.
Moved to ready to implement on the user's direction (in conversation, 2026-08-08): 'do those things' — the go-ahead for both remaining front-burner ideas.

Shipped as epic B9 (B9-1 /api/since/<hash>, B9-2 briefing banner). Verified live: returning visitor saw 'Since you last looked: 28 changes · 1 stale claim' expandable to card-level statements; dismiss advances the marker; first visit stores silently; rewritten-history marker resets quietly. Reused the ratify differ as predicted — effort was low.

title: Live reload — retire the clobber footgun
description: Server watches the data dir and pushes changes over SSE; the page re-renders from fresh state instead of clobbering hand/agent edits with its stale in-memory arrays.
context: The tool's top documented limitation (PROTOCOL §5, SKILL.md §4): if the page is open while an agent edits JSON, the page's next write overwrites the agent's work, so the skill has to say 'tell the user to reload'. fs.watch + one SSE route + a client refetch removes the standing warning.
compounding: An event channel from server to page is infrastructure: the briefing, save-indicator truthfulness, and any future multi-writer story ride on it. Explicitly the cheap alternative to the 'tiny service' the design avoided.
pros: Kills the one workflow rule that exists only to route around a defect
Small: fs.watch, one SSE endpoint, one client handler
Makes agent + open-UI coexistence safe — the actual daily usage
cons: Naive refetch can drop in-flight modal edits; needs a 'don't reload while modal open' guard
fs.watch has platform quirks (double events) — needs debounce

log.note: Captured from the capability brainstorm: quick win — directly retires the top documented limitation.

User green-lit the build in conversation (“build the refresh capabilities”). Shipped: fs.watch + debounce on the data dir, GET /api/events SSE route, client refresh with own-write echo skip and modal/drag/pending-save deferral. Contract docs updated to retire the reload warning.

title: Design drift curation pass
description: A curation pass that checks the UX specs in design/ against index.html: anchor grep, wireframe-vs-render skim, spec_state flags. Ships as AGENTS.md §7 pass 6 with the UX spec framework.
context: The UX spec framework (idea-ux-spec-framework) is only trustworthy if spec and UI provably move together. Three cheap mechanisms, no tooling: the spec_state frontmatter flag, a grep that every spec anchor resolves in index.html, and a curation pass that reports mismatches for the user to pick a fix direction.
pros: Keeps the spec framework honest for the cost of a grep
Same propose-then-approve posture as the other curation passes
cons: Wireframe-vs-render comparison is judgment, not mechanical — only anchors are provable

log.note: Being built now as part of the UX spec framework bootstrap — lands as curation pass 6 in AGENTS.md §7.
Done — pass 6 live in AGENTS.md §7; the anchor grep already caught and fixed one bad anchor during bootstrap.

title: Command palette and quick capture
description:
Keyboard-first operation: '/' opens a fuzzy palette over every epic, story, and idea — type a few letters, Enter, and you're on the card (the milestone-chip jump, generalized). 'n' captures a new idea from any page instantly. Capture is the funnel's mouth: any friction there loses ideas.

Technical shape: an overlay on the shared modal scrim; the index is built in-memory from state (id, title, type — no server change); subsequence fuzzy match with rank-by-match-quality; arrow keys + Enter navigation (the Milestones page's arrow-key pattern); Enter → goToEpic() / navigate() by type; 'n' → openIdea(null) from anywhere. Shortcuts suppressed while any input/textarea has focus.
context: Finding a card today means eyeballing lanes or setting filters; capturing an idea means navigating to the Ideas page first. Capture especially should be instant — ideas are the inbox, and the user brainstorms across tools (the copy-as-markdown flow), so the round-trip back into the board has to be one keystroke, not a navigation.
compounding: The jump-to-card machinery (goToEpic's filter+flash) generalizes to search results, and the in-memory index is the seed of cross-project search once one server serves all boards. Quick capture also makes every other surface cheaper to keep minimal — no page needs its own 'add' affordance to be reachable.
pros: Serves the heaviest interactive user (the human) daily
goToEpic already solved jump-and-highlight
cons: Fuzzy matching + palette UI is real surface area for a 1,100-line file
Keyboard shortcuts need care around inputs/modals (arrow-key precedent exists)

log.note: Captured from the capability brainstorm.
Promoted Later → Next: capture is the funnel's mouth and the user works the ideas inbox daily; friction there loses ideas. Jump-to-card also compounds with the growing card count.

Hardened: description restructured to plain + Technical shape (scrim overlay, in-memory index, subsequence fuzzy match, arrow-key pattern, focus-guarded shortcuts); context tied to the cross-tool brainstorm loop; compounding extended.
Moved to ready to implement on the user's direction (in conversation, 2026-08-08): 'do those things' — the go-ahead for both remaining front-burner ideas.

Shipped as epic B8 (B8-1 palette overlay + fuzzy jump, B8-2 'n' quick capture). Verified live: '/' opens focused from any page, subsequence ranking (epic/story/idea all jump correctly), shortcuts inert in fields and modals, Escape layer order, footer hints.

title: Ratify review panel — see what changed since last commit
description:
Before saying 'save', see exactly what you're ratifying: a review panel listing every board change since the last commit as card-level statements — 'O1-2 moved Doing → Done', 'idea-wip-gates-ui hardened, moved to ready for review', '2 cards reordered' — not raw diffs. Turns commit-=-ratify from an act of faith into an informed review, at the speed a human actually ratifies.

Technical shape: server shells out to git status --porcelain / git show HEAD:<file> on the data dir and diffs the JSON semantically (by card id and field, reorder-aware since array order is queue state) into change-summary lines served at /api/pending. UI: a pending-count badge on the 'saved' dot; click opens the panel. Rides the existing fs.watch/SSE pipeline, so the panel live-updates while agents work.
context: The culture is 'edit freely, commit = ratify' — but the human ratifies blind unless they drop to the terminal. This gets worse, not better, as the tool succeeds: agents now move cards in real time while building (AGENTS.md §6) and pages live-reload, so the volume of uncommitted churn between ratifications keeps growing. The live board shows changes as they happen; the review panel is the missing other half — the same changes as a reviewable set at the moment of ratification. Together they close the loop that makes git-as-only-persistence trustworthy at agent speed.
compounding: Two reusable capabilities in one: (1) the first server endpoint that reads git — the board briefing ('since you last looked') and history timeline ideas are the same read pointed at older commits; (2) the semantic JSON-diff-to-English summarizer, which the briefing reuses verbatim. Git stops being passive persistence and becomes a readable data source, which is also the foundation any future undo/blame affordance needs.
pros: Directly serves the board's central ritual (ratify) — the review step the convention always implied
Card-level semantic summaries, not raw diffs — readable at ratify speed
Git is already there — no new persistence, no new state
Live-updating via the existing SSE pipeline — zero new client machinery
Unlocks briefing + timeline: both reuse the git-read endpoint and the summarizer
cons: First feature that makes server.js shell out — small, deliberate growth of the 'tiny server' surface
Semantic diffing needs care: array reorders are meaningful (queue order) and must read as 'reordered', not as N edits

sections.title: Panel sketch
sections.body: Header area: the green 'saved' dot gains a pending count ('● 7 pending'). Click → slide-over panel, newest first, grouped by resource: Epics — 'O1-2 moved Doing → Done', 'O2-1 claimed by claude'; Ideas — 'idea-x → ready for review', 'front burner reordered'. Footer: 'save' hint naming the git commit that ratifies. Empty state: 'Everything ratified — board matches HEAD.' No buttons that write: the panel reviews, the human ratifies in conversation or terminal, same as today.

log.note: Captured from the capability brainstorm: compounding — makes the commit-=-ratify culture visible in the tool itself.

Hardened for review: raw git-diff panel upgraded to card-level semantic summaries (readable at ratify speed); tied to the live-board loop — real-time agent card moves make blind ratification the board's biggest remaining trust gap. Compounding sharpened: the git-read endpoint + JSON-diff summarizer are the shared foundation briefing and timeline reuse. Decision-ready: scope, surface sketch, and the one real cost (server shells out) are all on the card.

Moved to ready to implement on the user's direction (in conversation, 2026-08-08): 'implement the top 3 items with the best ROI on user value.' Ranked #1 — high impact on the core ritual, compounding double (git endpoint + semantic differ feed briefing and timeline).

Shipped as epic B3 (B3-1 /api/pending + semantic differ, B3-2 badge + review panel). Verified live: 23 pending statements on the real dirty board, combined move+edit statements, reorder as one line, live update while editing, clean/no-git/no-commit states, zero write affordances.

title: Ready queue — what agents can build right now
description:
The 'begin X' menu made visible: one flat queue of every story a human could hand to an agent right now — ready: true, epic unblocked and ungated, story unclaimed — grouped by epic and ranked the way the protocol ranks. Decompose-before-build made stories the unit of all work; this is where they surface.

Technical shape: a strip on the Board page beside Next up (same visual language), listing pickable stories as '[kind] B4-1 story name' chips grouped under their epic id; pickability = PROTOCOL §3 applied to stories (ready + epic deps done + epic gate open + unclaimed), ranked story priority index → epic rank → file order; click → the story modal. Pure client-side read of loaded state — no new data.
context: ready: true is the human's hand-off signal, but ready stories are buried inside per-epic modals (a count badge on cards is all the board shows). One flat queue answers 'what could I say begin to right now' — the story-level twin of the Next-up strip, and the natural landing surface after decompose-before-build turns every approved idea into stories.
compounding: Same pickability computation as the Next-up strip, applied at story grain — the two strips together make PROTOCOL §3 fully visible. The queue is also the natural anchor for any future one-click dispatch ('begin' from the browser) — the menu exists before the button does.
pros: Makes the human→agent hand-off surface explicit
Cheap if next-up lands first
cons: Another view to route/maintain — may be better as a section of the next-up panel than its own page

log.note: Captured from the capability brainstorm. Open question: own page vs a section of the next-up panel.
Rows mode (idea-board-swimlanes) now shows stories grouped by epic on the board itself, with ready ticks visible — this card stays open only for the flat, pickability-filtered 'begin menu' angle.
Promoted Later → Next: decompose-before-build just made stories the unit of all work — the 'begin X' menu is now a daily surface, not a nicety. Low effort, direct workflow enabler.

title: UX spec framework — the UI defined in markdown
description: Every screen described in a design/*.md spec: ASCII wireframe, components table anchored to real DOM ids/functions, interactions, states. Claude's Design workflow edits the spec first, then makes index.html match — spec and UI commit together.
context: The UI is 1,100 lines of hand-written vanilla JS with no durable statement of what it's supposed to be — every UX conversation re-derives it from code. A lightweight, visual, markdown spec set (in the spirit of arc-core's templates and AGENTS.md's role for data) gives human and agent a shared, diffable source of truth the AI can interpret to build changes through conversation.
compounding: Counts double: every future UI idea on this board (next-up, WIP badges, palette, switcher…) gets designed as a cheap spec edit before any code, reviewed in the same propose-then-approve loop as board data, with drift kept honest by the curation pass. It's the design analogue of AGENTS.md — infrastructure for all subsequent UX work.
pros: Design conversations produce a durable, diffable artifact
Wireframes reviewable by a human in any editor — no tooling
Anchors make spec-vs-code drift mechanically checkable
cons: Two artifacts must move together forever — discipline cost on every UI change
ASCII wireframes approximate layout; they can't capture visual polish

sections.title: Shape
sections.body: design/DESIGN.md is the contract (format, workflow loop, drift rules, non-goals). design/system.md names tokens and shared chrome; board.md, milestones.md, ideas.md, idea-detail.md each carry frontmatter (screen, route, spec_state: matches-ui | ahead-of-ui), an ASCII wireframe ≤80 cols with {curly} placeholders for config vocab, a components table whose Anchor column names real ids/functions in index.html, interactions (trigger → behavior → data effect), states, and data bindings. Deliberately NOT: a parseable DSL, codegen, a component library, pixel values, screenshots.

log.note: Being built now: bootstrap reverse-engineers the existing three pages into specs, adds the Design workflow to the skill, and curation pass 6 for drift.
Done and exercised: the Next-up panel shipped through the workflow — design/board.md spec updated together with index.html, ending matches-ui.

title: Rows mode — story swimlanes by epic
description: A board mode toggle (Epics | Rows). Epics mode is today's board, untouched. Rows mode shows one swimlane per epic — header with id, name, gate badge, done-count — and the epic's stories as compact draggable cards in the lane columns. Stories move across lanes within their row; cross-row drops and gated epics refuse.
notes: Stories inherit the epic's milestone/theme/tag filters; epics without stories are skipped in Rows mode (with a count note) so boards like chaim's 44-epic/0-story state don't render as empty rows. Preferred mode persists via the existing save-view chip (config.view.default_board_mode).
context: Stories never appear on the board today — only a count badge on the epic card; the stories themselves are buried in per-epic modals. The user asked directly for rows grouping similar stories, with the epic as the row. Story data already carries epic_id and column, so this is pure rendering plus story-level drag.
compounding: First surface where stories are directly manipulable — the ready queue, WIP badges on story lanes, and any future story-level flow ride on the same cells and drag wiring.
pros: Zero data-model change — stories already have epic_id and column
Epic board and its dependency/gate semantics stay untouched (toggle, not replace)
Substantially covers idea-ready-queue's board-surface half
cons: Story drag has no dependency guard analogue — only the epic gate constrains it
Second board rendering path to keep in sync with the spec

log.note: Captured from the user's direct request in conversation (rows grouping similar stories; epic as the row confirmed as the grouping). Toggle-not-replace and skip-empty-epics decided with the user; status ready to implement records that in-conversation thumbs-up. Building now via the Design workflow.

Done: shipped via the Design workflow — design/board.md + index.html together, spec_state back to matches-ui. Verified live against the demo board: toggle, swimlane render, story drag writing stories.json, gate/cross-row refusals wired, save-view persists default_board_mode, goToEpic falls back to Epics mode. Awaiting ratification (Design: + Board: commits) on save.

title: WIP limits and gates surfaced in the UI
description:
Make the board's own rules visible: lane headers show count vs limit and go red when over WIP; gated cards wear a lock chip naming their gate until a human opens it. The rules agents already obey stop being invisible to the human watching them work.

Technical shape: pure rendering from config the client already loads — wip_limits drives 'N/limit' lane counts with an over-limit state; a lock chip renders when gate ≠ 'none' and the gate isn't in open_gates. Advise, don't enforce: no drop is ever blocked — the UI informs, the human stays the authority, and enforcement remains the agent protocol's job (PROTOCOL §3). No new fields, no server changes.
context: Two config vocabularies (wip_limits, open_gates) govern agent behavior but are invisible in the UI they govern. The trust gap runs both ways: a human can drag a lane past its WIP limit without knowing, and can stare at a free-looking card wondering why no agent picks it — because the gate exists only in JSON. It matters more now that agents move cards through the lanes in real time while building: the human watches lanes fill live, and the board should show the rules the motion is obeying. Advise-only is the aligned answer to the old open question — the UI is a lens, not a policeman; a human deliberately overruling a limit is allowed and visible, not prevented.
compounding: First rendering of PROTOCOL state in the UI. The visual vocabulary it establishes — red over-limit counts, lock chips with gate names — is exactly what the next-up panel (pickability, the rest of PROTOCOL §3) will reuse, and it moves the board toward explaining itself: every rule an agent follows should be visible where humans look.
pros: Config fields already exist; pure client-side rendering — hours, not days
Explains agent behavior to the human — closes the 'why won't it pick this card' trust gap
Live feedback channel: with agents moving cards in real time, over-limit lanes light up as it happens
Advise-only resolves the enforce-vs-inform question in line with the tool's philosophy
cons: Advise-only means the board can show a rule being broken without stopping it — deliberate, but the over state must be loud enough to notice

log.note: Captured from the capability brainstorm.

Hardened for review: resolved the open advise-vs-enforce question (advise-only — the UI is a lens, enforcement stays in the agent protocol) and reframed around the live board: agents now move cards in real time, so surfaced limits/gates become live feedback on agent behavior, not static decoration. Impact raised medium → high: low effort + closes the human side of the protocol trust loop — this is the definition of a quick win.

Shipped as epic B1 (stories B1-1 lane WIP counts, B1-2 gate lock chips) — decomposed per the new build rule, criteria verified on a live board (over-limit red 2/0, at-limit 1/1, ⛔ chip clearing live when the gate opened, drops never blocked).

title: context_docs chips in the epic modal (read-only)
description:
Show an epic's reading list where decisions happen: context_docs render as labeled chips in the epic modal, and clicking a chip copies its path — ready to paste into an editor, a terminal, or another Claude session. Editing stays file/skill-only; the modal just finally shows what a builder must read.

Technical shape: reuse the Milestones page's ctxDocs renderer read-only inside the epic modal; chip click → navigator.clipboard.writeText(path) + confirmation toast, following the copy convention the Ideas page established. No new endpoint, no write path — AGENTS.md's 'no widget' stance holds.
context: 'Read the context before building' is the tool's core discipline, but the epic modal — where a human actually looks at a card — doesn't show what the context is. This bites hardest at the new decompose-before-build step: every ready-to-implement idea now becomes an epic the human reviews in this modal, and the reading list should be visible at exactly that moment. The ctxDocs renderer already exists for milestones; reusing it read-only respects the deliberate no-editor decision while making the discipline visible.
compounding: Establishes the read-only context-surface pattern — labeled chips + copy-to-clipboard — that the story modal's context and idea deep-dive context can reuse as-is. Also extends the board→other-tools flow the Ideas page's copy button started: the board keeps becoming the place you launch work from, without ever growing an editor.
pros: Renderer already exists (ctxDocs) — this is reuse, not construction
Surfaces the context stack at the exact moment of epic review (decompose-before-build made the modal the review surface)
Copy-on-click makes chips actionable without any server growth
Keeps the deliberate no-edit-widget boundary
cons: Chips copy, they don't open — an in-browser doc viewer would need a server file route, deliberately out of scope for now

log.note: Captured from the capability brainstorm.

title: History timeline — the board's git log as a page
description:
The board's ratification history as a page: every Board: commit with date, message, and what changed — the backlog's story, told by git. Turns the commit-=-ratify convention into a browsable product surface instead of a terminal-only artifact.

Technical shape: an /api/history endpoint (git log --format=… -- <data dir>, newest first, capped ~50) feeding a #/history page — one entry per ratification: relative date, message, files touched; expanding an entry lazily diffs that commit against its parent with the ratify panel's semantic differ, showing the same card-level statements. Nav tab beside Docs; read-only throughout.
context: The Board: commit convention means the project's history already narrates how the backlog evolved — but only in the terminal. A timeline page makes ratification history part of the product: 'when did we decide this' and 'what shipped last week' become clicks, and the convention itself becomes visible, which reinforces it.
compounding: Third consumer of the git-reading endpoint (after ratify review and briefing) — by this point git-as-data-source is fully amortized and every future git-backed surface (blame a card, undo a ratification) is an increment, not a project.
pros: Zero new persistence
Rewards the disciplined commit-message convention
cons: Read-only nice-to-have; lowest urgency of the git trio

log.note: Captured from the capability brainstorm. Sequenced last of the three git-reading ideas.

Hardened: description restructured to plain + Technical shape (/api/history via git log, lazy per-commit semantic diff on expand, nav tab beside Docs); context sharpened — making the convention visible reinforces it.

Confirmed as #3 of the top-3 ROI picks (user direction in conversation, 2026-08-08; the human had already dragged it to ready to implement): after the ratify panel ships the git endpoint + differ, the timeline's marginal effort drops to low — best marginal ROI on the list.

Shipped as epic B5 (B5-1 /api/history endpoints, B5-2 #/history page + design/history.md). Verified live: newest-first timeline with files touched, lazy cached per-commit card-level diffs (0 refetches), root-commit and no-commit states. Third consumer of the git-read capability, as predicted.

title: Milestone progress viz
description:
One aggregate bar per milestone answering 'how far along is this, overall' at a glance — plus a mini-bar per deliverable so the lagging one stands out. The Milestones page already knows the numbers; it just never draws them.

Technical shape: pure client-side aggregation over epicsOfMilestone() — bucket each mapped epic by lane position (first / middle / last), render a stacked bar with the existing lane color tokens (laneVar), a done-fraction label, and the same stacked mini-bar per deliverable row. Renders only when the milestone maps epics; no new data, no server change, no new tokens.
context: The Milestones page already rolls up done/total per deliverable; there's no at-a-glance answer to 'how far along is this milestone overall', and no way to spot the deliverable dragging it. One bar per milestone plus one per deliverable answers both without adding a single field.
compounding: The lane-bucket aggregation is the reusable piece: the same computation gives a per-epic story burnup on board cards, and — once multi-board serving exists — a cross-project progress rollup. Draw-a-stacked-bar-from-lane-buckets becomes a small shared primitive.
pros: All inputs already computed client-side
Makes the milestone tabs scannable
cons: Progress bars can imply precision the epic-count metric doesn't have

log.note: Captured from the capability brainstorm.

Hardened: description restructured to plain + Technical shape (lane-position bucketing, laneVar-colored stacked bars, per-deliverable mini-bars); empty compounding filled — the lane-bucket aggregation is a reusable primitive.

decision: Does the bar count epics or stories — and do archived (shipped) epics still count toward the total?

title: Board doctor — validate what the contract promises
description:
One command (and a quiet UI banner) that checks the board's data against the rules AGENTS.md already states: stories pointing at epics that don't exist, deps naming missing ids, themes/milestones outside the config vocab, milestone deliverables linking dead epics, duplicate ids. Report and offer fixes; never silently repair.

Technical shape: a pure function over the five loaded resources returning {severity, message, ids} — reused two ways: './board doctor' printing to the terminal for CI-ish use, and a dim '⚕ N issues' chip beside the pending badge that opens the list. No new data, no new endpoint (the client already holds every resource).
context: AGENTS.md §2/§3 state real invariants — ids are permanent, vocab comes from config, deliverable epics must exist — but nothing enforces them, and agents edit these files directly by design. arc's board is now 6 epics / 20 stories / 63 ideas / 5 milestones maintained mostly by agents; a dangling deliverable link or a theme typo degrades the milestone roll-up quietly, and the roll-up is what the human trusts to answer 'where are we'.
compounding: Turns the contract from prose into something checkable, which makes every future rule cheap to enforce (add a check, not a convention). Also the natural home for the 'is this board healthy' signals stale claims and drift both produce.
pros: Pure function over data already in memory — no schema, no endpoint
Protects the milestone roll-up, the board's most trusted number
Same check serves terminal and UI
cons: Report-only by design; auto-fix is tempting and deliberately out of scope until the reports prove boring

log.note: Captured from the session retrospective: the contract grew several new invariants (archived_at rules, decompose-before-build, real-time moves) with no way to check any of them.
Enriched for agent pickup: why-now, the open decision, conviction, build constraints and an acceptance boundary — so a builder can judge scope without reconstructing the reasoning from prose.

Shipped as B30. Decision answered: report-only always, and exit non-zero on errors only — a check that fails CI over a stale claim gets switched off. Validation plan written retroactively, since the card predates the rule that promotion requires one.

why_now: The contract gained several invariants in quick succession — archived_at rules, needs, promoted_to, decompose-before-build — and nothing checks any of them, while arc's board (10 epics, 39 stories, 60+ ideas) is maintained mostly by agents editing JSON directly.
decision: Report-only, or offer fixes? And should it exit non-zero so it can gate CI, or stay an on-demand human tool?
constraints: A pure function over the five loaded resources — no new endpoint, no schema. Never auto-repair: report and let a human or agent decide, the same stance gates take.
acceptance: ./board doctor names every violation with the ids involved, and the UI shows a quiet issue count that opens the same list; a clean board says so in one line.
validation: ./board doctor exits 1 on a board with a seeded duplicate id, orphan story, dangling deliverable, early archive and dep cycle, naming each; exits 0 on a clean board and on warnings alone; and the UI chip reports the identical counts and codes.

title: Dependency view — group the board by leverage
description:
A third lens beside Active/Archive: stop sorting by priority and group by what enables what. Foundations at the top (ideas nothing waits on but several things need), then the capabilities they unlock beneath — answering the roadmap question a priority list can't: what should I build next that makes several future things possible.

Technical shape: no graph library. Build the reverse-dependency index already used for the card leverage marker, then bucket: tier 0 = ideas with no unresolved deps that other ideas name; tier 1 = ideas depending only on tier 0; and so on (a simple topological layering, cycles broken by file order and flagged). Render as stacked labelled groups with an ↓ between tiers, reusing the existing idea cards. Read-only view; no new data.
context: arc's board is 23 active ideas where the most strategically valuable ones (temporal character state, prose-canon binding) look like ordinary features because their leverage is invisible. Priority ranking answers 'what is most urgent'; this answers 'what unlocks the most', which for a product still assembling its foundations is the more useful question. Proposed in the user's design critique (2026-08-09) as the highest-value board-level addition.
compounding: The tiering computation is the same one a 'critical path to milestone X' view would need, and the reverse index already ships in the card leverage marker — this is presentation over data the board already holds.
pros: Makes foundational work visibly foundational, which priority tiers cannot
Reuses the reverse-dependency index — no new data, no library
Answers the roadmap question the user actually asks
cons: Only earns its place on a board with real dependency density; a flat backlog shows one tier and learns nothing
Cycles need a defined, visible fallback rather than silent reordering

log.note: Captured from the user's design critique: 'That is more valuable for Arc than a conventional priority ranking.' Depends on the lens switcher landing first.
Enriched for agent pickup: why-now, the open decision, conviction, build constraints and an acceptance boundary — so a builder can judge scope without reconstructing the reasoning from prose.

Shipped as the Leverage lens on the ideas page. Foundations / Tier n / Standalone, stacked with connectors, computed from the ideas' own deps — no graph library, no new data, read-only, per the constraints. Two departures from the card, both deliberate: deps naming something outside the visible set (an epic, an archived idea) are informational and never hold a card back a tier; and a card that waits on nothing and that nothing waits on is listed separately as Standalone rather than sitting in tier 0, because leaving it there buried the handful of load-bearing cards the view exists to surface. Leverage now also renders on back-burner cards, which suppress it elsewhere. Built directly rather than promoted to an epic first (user instruction).

why_now: Every idea now shows what it Opens, but nothing ranks by it — so the foundational cards that several others wait on still read like ordinary features when you scan the column.
decision: Answered: cycles are flagged in place. A 'Cannot be placed' group names the loop (idea-a → idea-b → idea-a) rather than breaking it silently by file order — a cycle is a real backlog problem, and a view that hid it would be lying about the order it drew.
constraints: No graph library and no new data: reuse the reverse index behind unlockedBy(). Read-only view — tiers are a reading of the backlog, never an edit to it.
acceptance: Foundational ideas appear in a top tier with the capabilities they unlock beneath them, and any cycle is reported rather than hidden.

title: Project switcher in the header
description:
Switch between arc, chaim, and board from the header — one server serves every board registered in projects.json, no restart, no second port.

Technical shape: the server reads projects.json and scopes data routes by project (/api/<project>/board, /api/<project>/events), watching each active project's data dir; the client carries the project in the URL (e.g. #/board?p=arc or a path prefix) so links deep-link across boards, and the header dropdown re-fetches + re-renders via the existing applyBoard() path. Touches every data route plus the client fetch layer — honest medium effort.
context: Today ./board <name> binds the server to one data dir; comparing or hopping between project boards means a second port. With three projects registered and agents working several backlogs, switching is a daily motion, not an edge case — and the current workaround (PORT=4301) is exactly the kind of terminal detour the tool exists to remove.
compounding: Multi-board serving is the substrate for every cross-project surface: one 'everything I could work on' queue across arc + chaim + board, cross-project search in the command palette, a portfolio-level briefing. Nothing cross-project can exist before this does.
pros: projects.json already exists as the registry
Removes the PORT=4301 workaround
cons: Server becomes multi-tenant: routes need a project dimension, a real (if small) server.js change
BOARD_DATA_DIR env contract with the skill needs rethinking

log.note: Captured from the capability brainstorm — promoted from edge case to daily motion by this board's existence.

Hardened: description restructured to plain + Technical shape (route scoping by project, per-project watch, deep-linkable project in URL, applyBoard reuse); effort honestly kept medium — it touches every data route.

Promoted Later → Next with direct evidence: today's session hit the port-4300 collision (a board already running blocked ./board arc) and needed a second port to compare boards — exactly the friction this removes. ./board stop made the workaround bearable, not unnecessary.
Enriched for agent pickup: why-now, the open decision, conviction, build constraints and an acceptance boundary — so a builder can judge scope without reconstructing the reasoning from prose.

Decision answered and validation plan written, then promoted to B31 and groomed into four stories. One server scoping routes by project; project in the path prefix; single-project BOARD_DATA_DIR mode preserved untouched.

why_now: Three projects are registered and this session repeatedly ran two servers on two ports to compare boards — the collision that prompted ./board stop was this friction surfacing.
decision: Answered 2026-08-12: one server, routes scoped by project — nothing cross-project (a queue spanning boards, palette search, a portfolio briefing) can exist while a process sees one directory. The project sits in the path prefix (/arc/#/board), before the hash, so the server can read it without JavaScript and the hash router is untouched.
constraints: Single-project mode via BOARD_DATA_DIR must keep working untouched, and existing deep links must survive — the project belongs in the URL, not in hidden state.
acceptance: Switching projects from the header shows the other board without a restart, and a copied URL reopens the same project's page.
validation: With three projects registered: /arc/#/board and /board/#/ideas each serve their own data from one port; the header switcher moves between them without a restart and a copied URL reopens the same project on the same page; edits saved on one board do not appear on another; live refresh fires only for the project you are looking at; and BOARD_DATA_DIR=<dir> node server.js still serves an unprefixed single-project board with the skill's contract unchanged.

title: Docs as first-class citizens — a registry with two-way links
description: Keep PRFAQs/architecture/decision docs as markdown in the *-system-design repo, but give each identity in a thin registry: type (prfaq/architecture/decision/contract), status (draft/ratified/superseded), and the themes/milestones/epics it drives. Epics answer 'what vision justifies me'; a PRFAQ answers 'what work exists because of me' — the promoted_to trick, applied upstream. A vision doctor then checks drift: a ratified PRFAQ no epic advances, an epic no doc justifies, a cited section that no longer exists. The Docs tab grows from rendering CAPABILITIES.md to rendering the project's own library.

title: Attribution journal — who changed the working state, and undo
description: The server knows whether a write came through the UI (a click) or appeared on disk (an agent). Log every change to an append-only journal — source, timestamp, the same card-level statements the pending panel shows — and add '↩ revert this one' per unratified statement in the pending panel. Git protects ratified state; this covers the gap between saves, where a bad drag currently means hand-editing JSON.
notes: Captured from the supply-chain / CX brainstorm (2026-08-13).
context: Twice in one session the working state changed and nobody could account for it (idea-board-doctor moved to ready-for-review; B23 archived at 12:21) — commits had to name changes as 'not mine'. That is a trust leak in a tool whose premise is that the human ratifies what they see.
compounding: The journal is the substrate for presence ('2 agents active'), per-change revert, and honest briefings.
why_now: Two unattributed changes in one session is the evidence; the pending panel already renders the statements a journal would store.
